question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old retired postal clerk, gravida 3 para 3, walked into the emergency department at 11:15 complaining that for the last 18 hours every bowel movement “looked like tar spilled on the pavement,” coated the porcelain, emitted a pungent metallic odor, and was difficult to rinse away despite multiple flushes; the most recent episode occurred in the triage lavatory only minutes before her vital signs were obtained and again produced a thick, shiny, coal-black stool that clung to the bowl and turned the test card positive for occult blood within seconds. She reports mild crampy discomfort in the epigastrium radiating toward the left costal margin and an acrid taste at the back of her throat but denies regurgitating blood of any color, denies seeing coffee-ground material in vomitus, and denies red streaks on toilet paper, bright red blood per rectum, or hematochezia. She explicitly states she has not felt dizzy, had tunnel vision, or actually fainted at any point today; she drove herself from home after calling her daughter for advice, parked in the visitor lot without difficulty, and ambulated briskly to the check-in window. The patient has a past medical history of well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with metformin 1 000 mg twice daily, long-standing essential hypertension treated with amlodipine 10 mg each morning, chronic knee osteoarthritis for which she takes over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg three times daily “for the last couple of weeks” because spring gardening aggravated her joints, and hyperlipidemia on rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly. She has no prior endoscopic evaluations, has never required hospitalization for gastrointestinal complaints, and her last primary-care laboratory panel obtained eight months ago reportedly showed normal creatinine and hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL. She has never been prescribed anticoagulants, antiplatelet therapy beyond a baby aspirin that she stopped two years ago due to reflux, corticosteroids, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and she uses no herbal supplements or energy drinks. She quit smoking 12 years ago after a 20-pack-year history and drinks a single lager on Saturday evenings while watching televised baseball; she denies recreational drug use. Family history is notable for a brother with celiac disease and a mother who died of stroke at 80; there is no known family history of bleeding disorders or gastric malignancy. Review of systems today is negative for fever, chills, weight loss, night sweats, pruritus, jaundice, cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, lower-extremity edema, skin bruising, hematuria, or dark urine. She has been nil per os since a light dinner of grilled chicken and rice the evening before because of queasiness. On arrival—prior to intravenous access, crystalloid infusion, vasoactive medication, acid suppression, antiemetic, or blood transfusion—she was seated upright on the stretcher, conversant and oriented, with cool dry skin and an occasionally furrowed brow. Manual vital signs taken with her left arm supported at heart level revealed a systolic blood pressure of 151 mm Hg, diastolic 86 mm Hg, and a narrow pulse pressure; the cardiac monitor displayed a regular sinus tachycardia at 147 beats per minute that matched her rapid radial pulse; respirations were 18 per minute and unlabored; oral temperature measured 36.7 °C; oxygen saturation was 97 % while breathing ambient air. Capillary refill was three seconds, palpebral conjunctivae appeared pale, sclerae were anicteric, and oral mucosa was moist without telangiectasias or petechiae. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated at 30°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruits, and peripheral pulses were rapid but symmetric without pitting edema. Cardiac auscultation noted tachycardic S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal excursion. The abdomen was flat, not distended, tympanitic to percussion; gentle palpation produced modest tenderness in the mid-epigastrium without guarding, rebound, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. Skin examination revealed no spider angiomas, palmar erythema, purpura, or ecchymoses. Focused neurologic screening showed alert mentation, equal reactive pupils, intact extraocular movements, symmetric facial strength, 5/5 power in all extremities, and steady finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements. Digital rectal examination produced a copious smear of glossy black stool with characteristic tarry consistency and pungent iron odor. A single 18-gauge peripheral catheter was then placed exclusively for diagnostic blood sampling and type-and-screen; at that precise snapshot she had received no therapeutic interventions. Stat laboratory studies resulted 14 minutes later—still before any treatment—including hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, hematocrit 27 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 214 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 10.1 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 78 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.04; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and albumin were pending at note time. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained concurrently confirmed sinus tachycardia at 146 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright portable chest radiography displayed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette; a single-view supine abdominal radiograph revealed a nonspecific bowel gas pattern without free intraperitoneal air or obstructive features. She remains fasting, connected to continuous telemetry and pulse-oximetry monitoring, while expedited esophagogastroduodenoscopy is being arranged to localize and control the presumed upper gastrointestinal source of her profuse black stools and anemia.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses pre-endoscopic findings in suspected upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Before treatment:
- Blood urea nitrogen: 78 mg/dL, above the highest-tier threshold of 70 mg/dL (urea ≥25 mmol/L) → 6.
- Hemoglobin: 9.0 g/dL in a woman, below 10 g/dL → 6.
- Systolic blood pressure: 151 mm Hg, at least 110 → 0.
- Pulse: 147/min, at least 100 → 1.
- Melena: black, tarry stool confirmed on rectal examination → 1.
- Syncope: explicitly denied → 0.
- Hepatic disease: none documented → 0.
- Cardiac failure: none documented → 0.
Sum: 6 + 6 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 14.
Final answer: 14
